abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: This Phase 1, open‐label, 2‐part, single‐dose study aimed to investigate the pharmacokinetics, metabolism, and excretion of xevinapant, a small molecule inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs), in healthy male subjects. Part 1 focused on determining the mass balance recovery, pharmacokinetics, and metabolic profile of [14C]xevinapant following a single oral dose of 200 mg. Part 2 aimed to determine the absolute oral bioavailability of xevinapant by evaluating the pharmacokinetics of an oral dose of 200 mg xevinapant in comparison to an intravenous microtracer dose of [14C]xevinapant using accelerator mass spectrometry. After oral administration, xevinapant was rapidly absorbed, with a median time to maximum concentration of 0.5 h and a geometric mean half‐life of 13.2 h. The principal route of excretion of drug‐related material was fecal, accounting for 60.2% of the administered dose, while 33.3% was excreted in urine. Renal clearance accounted for 18.4% of total clearance. In addition to xevinapant, seven metabolites were structurally characterized in the samples analyzed. The principal route of metabolism was dealkylation to form metabolite D‐1143‐MET1, with secondary metabolism by oxidation. The major circulating components in plasma were xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1 (inactive on IAPs), which represented 28% and 42% of the total drug‐related exposure, respectively. The absolute oral bioavailability of xevinapant was determined to be 57.8%. The clearance of [14C]xevinapant was 12.2 L/h and the volume of distribution at steady‐state was 75.3 L. Xevinapant was well tolerated in healthy male subjects, with no clinically significant findings in clinical laboratory evaluations, vital signs, ECG, or physical examinations.

body.p: Resistance of tumor cells to death is a major challenge in current cancer treatments. 1 Abnormal expression of anti‐apoptotic molecules is one of the most frequent mechanisms resulting in apoptosis‐resistance, rendering current anticancer therapies less effective or ineffective. Therefore, reactivation of cancer cell death programs in cancer is a promising strategy to overcome treatment resistance. 1 , 2 , 3

Xevinapant is a small‐molecule inhibitor of IAPs (inhibitor of apoptosis proteins), which are key regulators of cell death and survival. IAP proteins comprise a family of anti‐apoptotic proteins that promote pro‐survival signaling pathways and prevent activation of the effector phase of apoptosis by interfering with activation of caspase. IAP overexpression is frequent in cancer and has been linked with poor prognosis, tumor progression, and treatment failure. 4 Drugs targeting and inhibiting IAPs can be useful to induce cell death or to lower the threshold for cell death induction when combined with other anticancer therapies like chemotherapies, targeted agents, or radiotherapy (RT). By inhibiting IAPs, xevinapant promotes apoptosis in cancer cells, making it a potential therapeutic agent for the treatment of various cancers. 5 Xevinapant was shown to significantly improve efficacy outcomes in combination with chemoradiotherapy (CRT) versus matched placebo plus CRT in a small randomized phase 2 study of patients with unresected locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck (SCCHN). However, xevinapant plus standard‐of‐care CRT did not show improved efficacy versus CRT alone in the randomised phase 3 TrilynX study (NCT04459715). In fact, a detrimental effect on efficacy and safety was observed when adding xevinapant to CRT, and the study was therefore terminated in June 2024. 6

The clinical pharmacology profile of xevinapant has been partially characterized in early‐phase trials. Following oral administration, the compound was rapidly absorbed, achieving maximal plasma concentrations within 1 to 3 h. 7 Pharmacokinetic (PK) analysis indicated a dose‐proportional exposure and no significant drug accumulation upon repeated administration. Furthermore, xevinapant demonstrated favorable distribution in tumor tissues. 8 A main circulating metabolite, D‐1143‐MET1, was identified early in the development and tested inactive against IAPs. Finally, a dedicated Phase 1 study in healthy participants indicated no meaningful impact of food or concomitant proton pump inhibitor (PPI) on xevinapant exposure. The trial also supported an overall similar PK profile across both healthy volunteers and the patient population. 9

As part of xevinapant clinical development, this Phase 1 study aimed to determine the mass balance and routes of elimination of xevinapant and characterize the metabolites in human plasma, urine, and feces following a single oral dose of [14C]xevinapant. In addition, the study aimed to further characterize the pharmacokinetics of xevinapant and its main metabolite D‐1143‐MET1 as well as to determine the oral bioavailability of xevinapant following oral and intravenous administration, respectively. Overall, this study provides quantitative and mechanistic information on the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of xevinapant in humans.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p:
This was a Phase 1, open‐label, non‐randomized, single‐dose study in healthy male subjects conducted in a single center in the UK (Labcorp, Leeds) in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the ethics committee (London‐Brent Research Ethics Committee). Permission to perform the study was also granted by the Administration of Radioactive Substances Advisory Committee. The study was divided into two parts:
Part 1 = Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME): Focused on determining the mass balance recovery, pharmacokinetics, and metabolic profile of [14C]xevinapant (Figure 1) following a single oral dose of 200 mg as a solution. Subjects were admitted on Day‐1, dosed on Day 1 and confined to the study site until at least Day 8. Subjects were discharged from the study site on Day 8, if the following discharge criteria were met: > 90% mass balance recovery, < 1% of the total radioactive dose was recovered in combined excreta (urine and feces) in two consecutive 24‐h periods, and plasma radioactivity levels below the limit of quantitation for liquid scintillation counting in two consecutive collections. If discharge criteria were not met on Day 15, subjects were required to continue collection of urine and feces on an outpatient basis on Day 22 and Day 29.
Part 2 = Absolute bioavailability (aBA): Aimed to determine the absolute oral bioavailability of xevinapant by evaluating the pharmacokinetics of an oral dose of 200 mg xevinapant in comparison to an intravenous (IV) microtracer dose of [14C]xevinapant using AMS. Subjects were admitted into the study site on Day‐1 and discharged on Day 5.
Safety and tolerability were monitored throughout the study.

sec.title: Subjects
sec.p: Healthy male subjects aged 18–45 years with a body mass index (BMI) of 18–30 kg/m2 were enrolled in the study. As there was no data suggesting that the metabolism of xevinapant was different in females versus males, female subjects were excluded from the study. This follows the “as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) principle” prescribed by the International Commission on Radiological Protection, 10 if no specific reason exists to include females, only male subjects should be included in studies involving radioactive material. Subjects were required to be in good health, as determined by medical history, physical examination, vital signs, ECG, and clinical laboratory evaluations. All subjects provided written informed consent before study screening. Participants were screened for inclusion up to 28 days prior to the first dose of study drug. Inclusion and exclusion criteria can be found in the Supporting Information.

sec.title: Dose Rationale
sec.p: The compound was administered orally at the intended therapeutic dose of 200 mg as a solution. A single dose of 200 mg had been shown to be safe and tolerated in healthy volunteers. 9 In part 1, the radioactive dose was 3.7 MBq (100 µCi). It was determined following review of nonclinical quantitative whole‐body autoradiography data and the consequent human dosimetry prediction. While this dosimetry supported a radioactive dose as high as 4.6 MBq, 3.7 MBq was selected based on the ALARA principle after a careful review of the expected concentration levels and the respective sensitivity of the radioanalytical methods to ensure detection and quantification of metabolites representing 10% of total drug‐related exposure. The effective dose was less than 1 mSv and fell within International Commission on Radiological Protection Guidelines for Category IIa studies (0.1–1 mSv). The radioisotope was at a chemically and metabolically stable position. In part 2, an IV microdose of [14C]xevinapant was administered 1 h after the oral dose as a bolus injection containing approximately 7.4 kBq (0.2 µCi). This dose was selected based on the expected radioactive concentrations after IV administration, as well as accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) sensitivity and dynamic range. Counterintuitively, the highest authorized dose was not the preferred one: for optimal AMS quantification, high 14C levels requiring sample dilution (notably in the excreta) must be avoided since they may lead to additional variability or even bias in the results.

sec.title: Sample Collection
sec.p: In part 1, K2EDTA blood samples for pharmacokinetic analysis, radioanalysis, and metabolite profiling and identification were collected serially at predose and up to 168 h postdose. These samples were also used for assessment of blood‐to‐plasma ratios and free fractions of total radioactivity, xevinapant, and D‐1143‐MET1. Urine and feces for evaluation of excretion kinetics, radioanalysis, and metabolite profiling and identification were collected predose and until 168 h postdose in 0 to 12 h, 12 to 24 h, and then 24 h time intervals at least until Day 8, and then up to discharge (max Day 15). Expired air was collected at defined timepoints during 48 h postdose in order to provide an estimate of the percentage of dose eliminated via 14CO2. This was a standard, precautionary approach to ensure a complete radioactivity recovery, and not resulting from an anticipated or identified metabolic pathway leading to 14CO2 excretion. Detailed methodologies can be found in the Supporting Information.

In part 2, blood samples for xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1 pharmacokinetics were collected serially up to 96 h post oral dose. Blood samples for [14C]xevinapant, [14C]D‐1143‐MET1, and total radioactivity pharmacokinetics were collected at predose and up to 95 h post IV dose. Urine and feces for pharmacokinetic and radioanalysis were collected predose up to 96 h post oral dose in 0 to 12, 12 to 24 h, and then daily time intervals.

sec.title: Analytical Methods for Total Radioactivity, Bioanalytics, and Metabolite Profiling and Identification
sec.p: Total radioactivity for part 1 in blood, plasma, plasma dialysate, urine, and feces was determined by LSC at LabCorp (Harrogate, UK).

Total radioactivity for part 2 in plasma, urine, and homogenized feces was analyzed by AMS at TNO (Leiden, The Netherlands) using an automated CO2‐combustion AMS method, developed and qualified for the quantitative analysis of 14C activity in human matrices, based on 14C/12C isotope ratios. 11

Xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1 were analyzed in plasma and urine by validated LC‐MS/MS assays with a concentration range from 2.5 to 2500 ng/mL for plasma using 50 µL plasma, and 50 to 50,000 ng/mL in urine using 10 µL stabilized urine (Tween 20 at 0.5% (v/v)).

For the determination of the plasma protein binding, xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1 were analyzed in plasma dialysate using a qualified LC‐MS/MS assay in a concentration range from 2.5 to 2500 ng/mL using 50 µL plasma dialysate.

The UPLC+AMS method used to quantify [14C]xevinapant for part 2 in human plasma was qualified according to the European Bioanalysis Forum recommendations, 12 and was also applied to quantify the 14C‐labeled metabolite D‐1143‐MET1.

Metabolite profiling was performed using an LC‐MS method coupled to offline microplate scintillation counting using an HTC PAL fraction collector (CTC Analytics AG, Switzerland) with TopCount NXT (Perkin Elmer LAS (UK) Ltd.). The eluent was split between the MS detector and fraction collector (30:70) for quantitative metabolite profiling. Structure elucidation of metabolites was performed on a Q Exactive Plus mass spectrometer with an electrospray ionization source (Thermo Scientific, UK).
Detailed methodologies can be found in the Supporting Information.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics (PK) Parameters
sec.p: PK parameters were derived using Phoenix WinNonlin (version 8.1) and calculated using non‐compartmental analysis, as presented in Table 4. Total radioactivity and D‐1143‐MET1 concentrations are given in ng or pg equivalents (Eq) of xevinapant/mL. The sum of metabolite‐to‐parent ratio was calculated as total radioactivity—[14C]xevinapant relative to [14C]xevinapant. The mean and percent coefficient of variation (CV%) data in plasma are provided as geometric mean and % geometric CV (%GeoCV) unless otherwise specified.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Safety assessments and analyses in both parts 1 and 2 consisted of monitoring and recording adverse events (AEs), including serious AEs and AEs of special interest; performing safety laboratory assessments; measuring vital signs; and conducting other tests (including ECGs and physical examinations). All participants who received at least one dose of xevinapant were included in the safety analyses.

sec.title: Subjects
sec.p: Twelve subjects (six subjects in Part 1 and six subjects in Part 2) were enrolled, dosed, and completed the study in accordance with the protocol.

sec.title: Part 1—ADME
sec.p: The mean plasma concentration–time profiles for xevinapant, D‐1143‐MET1, and total radioactivity following a single oral dose of 200 mg [14C]xevinapant are shown in Figure 2, and the associated PK parameters are summarized in Table 1. Xevinapant was rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with a median time to maximum concentration (tmax) of 0.5 h. After reaching Cmax, plasma concentrations of xevinapant and total radioactivity appeared to decline in a multiphasic manner through the last quantifiable concentration. The mean t1/2 for xevinapant, D‐1143‐MET1, and total radioactivity in plasma were 13.2, 7.69, and 18.7 h, respectively. Ratios for total radioactivity in whole blood relative to plasma were 0.472 and 0.571 for AUCinf and Cmax (Table 2), respectively, indicating little to no association of radioactivity with red blood cells. The mean unbound fractions of the xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1 in plasma were on average 14.7% and 10.3%, respectively, and constant over time. The mean (CV) AUCinf ratio of plasma xevinapant to total radioactivity was 0.194 (15.6%), indicating the presence of circulating metabolites, which was confirmed by the metabolite profiling and identification results presented in Table 3. The mean (CV) metabolite‐to‐parent ratios for the sum of metabolites in plasma relative to xevinapant were 4.15 (19.2%) for AUCinf and 0.505 (25.0%) for Cmax.

sec.p: In general, between‐subject variability following IV administration was low for AUCinf and Cmax for plasma radioactivity, plasma [14C]xevinapant, and plasma [14C]D‐1143‐MET1, with values ranging from 4.8% to 22.1%.

sec.title: Part 1—ADME
sec.p: After oral administration, the arithmetic mean of total radioactivity recovery in urine and feces was 93.5% of the administered radioactive dose. The mean cumulative recovery of radioactivity from the six subjects is shown graphically in Figure 4. Individual total recovery of total radioactivity ranged between 81.2% and 98.7%. The duration of collection was 192 h (N = 3), 216 h (N = 2), or 336 h (N = 1) as per discharge criteria. The majority (79.6%) of total radioactivity was excreted during the first 72 h after [14C]xevinapant administration.

caption.p: Arithmetic mean (± S.D.) cumulative recovery of total radioactivity following a single oral dose of [14C]xevinapant (200 mg, 3.7 MBq) expressed as a percentage of the administered dose in excreta. Dashed line: 90% and 100% recovery

sec.p: The primary route of excretion of total radioactivity was via feces, with 60.2% (arithmetic mean value; range 53.5% to 66.8%) of the dose recovered in this matrix. The remainder of total radioactivity was excreted via urine with an arithmetic mean of 33.3% (range 27.6% to 40.0%). No radioactivity was detected in expired air, indicating that the position of the radiolabel was stable.

sec.title: Part 2—aBA
sec.p: During the 0‐ to 96‐h collection period following IV administration, 73.8% of total radioactivity was recovered in urine and feces, with arithmetic mean values of 40.6% in urine (range: 34.5% to 46.8%) and 33.2% in feces (range: 11.4% to 39.7%), respectively. Arithmetic mean values for total cumulative recovery for [14C]xevinapant in urine and feces were 14.9% and 0.351%. Values for total cumulative recovery for [14C]D‐1143‐MET1 in urine and feces were 13.2% and 13.5%, respectively. Based on the total clearance of 12.2 L/h, renal clearance of xevinapant (2.25 L/h) was estimated to contribute 18.4% to its total systemic clearance.

sec.title: Metabolism
sec.p: The mean extraction recovery of radioactivity in the final plasma sample extracts was 96.5%; the mean final extraction recovery of radioactivity in feces extracts (89.0%) was also acceptable.

Metabolite profiling identified 27 radioactive components in plasma, 17 in urine, and 39 in feces (see Figure 5). The metabolite structures of all radioactive components that accounted for > 3% of the total radioactive exposure (AUC24h) in plasma, > 1% of the administered dose excreted in urine or > 3% of the administered dose excreted in feces were proposed based on retention time, MS/MS fragmentation, and/or comparison to reference compounds (D‐1143‐MET1).

caption.p: Representative metabolite profiles in plasma, urine, and feces pools

sec.p: The major circulating components in plasma were xevinapant and its dealkylated metabolite D‐1143‐MET1, representing 28% and 42% of the total radioactivity exposure, respectively. Overall, the values generated by metabolite profiling for both analytes were within the range of the PK parameters derived using LC‐MS/MS concentrations of xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1. Apart from the main metabolite D‐1143‐MET1, oxidated D‐1143‐MET1 accounted for 9% of the total drug‐related exposure, while all other plasma metabolites accounted for less than 3%. The half‐life of the oxidated D‐1143‐MET1 (15.9 h) was longer than that of the half‐lives determined for xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1 (see Table 1).

The metabolite profiles of whole blood samples taken at 4 h were comparable to the corresponding plasma profiles. Mean blood‐to‐plasma ratios of xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1 ranged between 0.42 and 0.58, indicative of no or limited binding to red blood cells. These values correspond to the blood‐to‐plasma ratio of total radioactivity (Table 2) as well as to blood‐to‐plasma ratios determined in vitro (data on file).

In pooled urine samples, the main components were xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1, which accounted for 10.4% and 14.4% of the administered dose, respectively. These numbers, estimated by metabolite profiling, were confirmed by the cumulative percentage of dose excreted (fe) for xevinapant (10.3%) and D‐1143‐MET1 (14.3%) derived by the LC‐MS/MS assay in urine. All other metabolites detected in urine accounted for less than 1% of the administered dose.

In feces, xevinapant was a minor component accounting for less than 1% of the administered dose. Metabolite D‐1143‐MET1 was the most abundant component in feces and represented 16% of the total administered dose. Oxidated D‐1143‐MET1 represented 6% of the administered dose. All other metabolites detected in feces accounted individually for less than 5% of the administered dose.
The proposed metabolic pathways for xevinapant in humans are summarized in Figure 6. The metabolites are listed in Table 4.

sec.title: Absolute Bioavailability
sec.p: Following administration of a single oral dose of 200 mg xevinapant and an IV microtracer of [14C]xevinapant, the absolute bioavailability of xevinapant based on mean plasma AUCinf following a single oral dose of 200 mg xevinapant administered as an oral solution was 57.8%. For individual subjects, the absolute oral bioavailability ranged from 51.6% to 63.3%.
A graphical representation of the proposed disposition of xevinapant following a single oral administration to healthy volunteers is summarized in Figure 7.

sec.title: Safety and Tolerability
sec.p: Xevinapant and [14C]xevinapant were well tolerated in healthy male subjects. Six subjects had a total of 10 treatment‐emergent adverse events (TEAEs) during the study, of whom two subjects had TEAEs that were classified as treatment‐related by the investigator. The only TEAEs that were reported by > 1 subject (across both parts of the study) were catheter site‐related reaction (originally reported as injection site reaction) and oropharyngeal pain, each of which were reported by two subjects. All TEAEs were mild in severity and had resolved by the end of the study. There were no clinically significant findings in clinical laboratory evaluations, vital signs, ECG, or physical examinations. Two subjects had local tolerability reactions related to the IV bolus, both of which had resolved by 2 h postdose; see the summary of treatment‐emergent adverse events (Table 5).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This human ADME study characterized the absolute bioavailability, mass balance, routes of excretion, clearance mechanisms, and biotransformation pathways, and metabolite profiles of the investigational IAP inhibitor xevinapant that was under clinical development for the treatment of SCCHN.

The PK profiles of xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1 in plasma after oral administration of [14C]xevinapant were comparable to the profiles obtained in previous studies in healthy volunteers and cancer patients. 7 , 9 This supported the applicability of the ADME results obtained from this study in healthy volunteers as being relevant for the broader clinical development program of xevinapant.

This study demonstrated that xevinapant is rapidly absorbed and metabolized, with a significant portion of the dose excreted via feces: mass balance was achieved between 192 and 336 h, with 93.5% of the radioactive dose recovered in excreta, including 60.2% as fecal excretion. The monitoring of expired air showed no radioactivity and supported that no biotransformation(s) involving loss of the radiolabeled carbon were missed. Recovery of 73.8% of the IV microtracer over a 4‐day period was slightly lower than the mass balance 96 h after oral administration (86.7%), for unknown reasons.

Based on the PK and metabolite profiles after a single oral administration of 200 mg [14C]xevinapant, the major circulating components in plasma were xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1, which represented 28% and 42% of the total radioactivity exposure (mean AUC24h), respectively. Six additional metabolites besides D‐1143‐MET1 were structurally elucidated (Figure 6). Oxidated D‐1143‐MET1 accounted for 9% of the total drug‐related exposure in plasma, while all the other radioactive components accounted each individually for less than 3% (based on mean AUC24h). The longer half‐life of total radioactivity compared to that of xevinapant could be explained by the half‐life of metabolites such as oxidated D‐1143‐MET1. Consequently, oxidated D‐1143‐MET1 may potentially represent a higher percentage of total drug‐related exposure at steady‐state.

The main components excreted via the urine were xevinapant and D‐1143‐MET1, which accounted for 10% and 14% of the administered dose, respectively. In feces, xevinapant accounted for less than 1% of the administered dose. D‐1143‐MET1 was the most abundant component in feces with 16% of the total administered dose. Minor metabolites in urine and feces were primarily further oxidated and/or dehydrogenated metabolites of D‐1143‐MET1. This data supported that the principal route of metabolism was by dealkylation to form D‐1143‐MET1, although the exact mechanism of its formation remains unclear and is a subject of further investigations. 14 Further metabolism was by oxidation of D‐1143‐MET1, as well as minor direct oxidation of xevinapant. A graphical representation of the proposed disposition of xevinapant following oral administration to healthy volunteers is summarized in Figure 7.

While the mean unbound fraction of xevinapant determined in this study (14.7% in ex vivo plasma dialysates) was in line with in vitro data (15.8% in dialysates spiked with xevinapant; data on file), the mean unbound fraction of D‐1143‐MET1 (10.3%) determined ex vivo in this study was ≈3‐fold lower as compared to the in vitro value (35.4%). A potential explanation for this discrepancy might be a too short equilibrium time in the in vitro study. Therefore, the unbound fractions determined ex vivo were considered to be definitive values to calculate unbound drug exposure metrics for safety and/ or drug‐drug interaction risk assessments.

The absolute oral bioavailability of xevinapant was determined to be 57.8%. The fraction absorbed was assumed to be high (> 90%), based on the criteria described in ICH M9, 15 , 16 on < 1% unchanged drug and stability of xevinapant in feces (data on file).

A single dose of xevinapant, as evaluated in this study, was well tolerated in healthy male subjects, with only mild adverse events reported, which resolved by the end of the study. This was in good agreement with safety data published from previous clinical trials. 9

The study revealed a novel circulating metabolite, that is, oxidated D‐1143‐MET1, representing 9% of total drug exposure, which was not detected in previous cold metabolite identification experiments (data on file). Accordingly, characterization of its metabolic formation and chemical structure, potential primary and secondary pharmacological effects warrant further investigations. 17 , 18 Furthermore, the data generated in this study were used to inform PBPK modeling for the DDI assessment and provide further insight into the potential impact of intrinsic and extrinsic factors (e.g., concomitant medications, organ impairment) on the PK and safety/efficacy profile of xevinapant.

In summary, the results of this study showed that xevinapant’ s disposition and elimination is mainly mediated by metabolism with only minor amounts of unchanged drug detected in excreta (∼10% in urine and < 1% in feces), whereas a total of 39 and 17 radioactive components were found in feces and urine, respectively, summing up in total to ∼88% of the administered dose. Safety of xevinapant was in well accordance with outcomes from previous clinical studies. In addition, the results of this study, together with in vitro metabolism data, provide the basis for a thorough understanding of xevinapant’ s human elimination pathways. These results were instrumental for characterizing the clinical pharmacology profile of xevinapant and further inform the right conclusion on drug–drug interaction and organ impairment considerations.
